Before you present this as a success, look closer at the two children who reliably land on red. A chart where most children never move and a small minority repeatedly land on public sanction isn't evidence of behaviour change — it's evidence of who's easiest to sort. Research on public clip/colour charts links them to increased shame and anxiety, disproportionate targeting of children with ADHD, trauma histories or SEND, and no lasting change in the behaviour they flag. The calm you're seeing may reflect compliance from fear rather than the outcome you want written up as pedagogy. If your head wants a write-up, be honest that two children have effectively become the chart's permanent function, and state what you're doing differently for them specifically. Otherwise you're publishing a case study for a practice most current guidance recommends retiring.

blunt_right: Check three sources before anything else. 1) SEC/state-registered advisers: adviserinfo.sec.gov (IAPD) — search his name and the firm; it shows registration status, disclosures, and any regulatory actions. 2) Brokers: brokercheck.finra.org — same idea if he sells securities or insurance products rather than acting as an adviser. 3) Arizona-specific: the Arizona Corporation Commission Securities Division (azcc.gov) regulates advisers operating in-state and handles complaints — call them directly and ask if there are any complaints or enforcement actions tied to his name or the firm. If he claims to be a CFP, verify at letsmakeaplan.org. A firm he keeps naming that doesn't show up in any of these is a strong red flag on its own. Sourcing clients through a church, building trust before pitching, and pressuring for large transfers without transparent paperwork is a classic affinity-fraud pattern targeting seniors. Also contact Arizona Adult Protective Services (1-877-767-2385) now — you don't need proof of fraud to file a report, only reasonable concern, and they can open a file before more money moves.
